title: The National Championship Where 750 Teens Get Down and Dirty—Literally
summary:
Imagine a championship where the playing field is a pit of red clay, the equipment is a water bottle, and the goal is to judge dirt. That's exactly what 750 high school students did at the National Land and Range Judging Contest in El Reno, Oklahoma. Members of 4-H and FFA (Future Farmers of America) traveled from across the country to scrutinize soil—testing its fertility, texture, and permeability—skills crucial for agriculture, construction, and environmental science.

The contest, nearly 75 years old, sends students to four undisclosed fields. At each, they have 25 minutes to evaluate the land's slope, erosion risk, and suitability for crops, grazing, or building. They scrape the soil, measure layers, and squirt water to see how fast it drains. Their observations are compared to professional assessments; the closest match wins.

For Clay Cash, a freshman from eastern Kentucky, this was a dream come true. He's been judging soil since fourth grade on his family's farm. Last year, his team won the state championship, earning a spot at nationals. They drove 15 hours to compete. "It's a very big deal for me," Cash said. "My sister got really close to making it here. I'm glad I could kind of fulfill that dream for us."

Maddie Willis, a junior from Indiana, sees the contest as more than science. "I love being able to say that I play in dirt," she said. "It's amazing to meet all these people from around the world and make new friends."

Soil management specialist DeAnn Presley emphasizes the real-world stakes. Understanding soil helps determine everything from crop viability to where to lay railroad tracks. Coordinator Larry Wright, involved since 1978, says the contest recognizes a valuable skill. "These individuals have a skill that is valuable," he said, comparing it to sports in terms of recognition.

In an era of screens and virtual experiences, this contest is refreshingly tactile. Students get low to the ground, hands caked in mud, using observation and reasoning. It's a reminder that beneath our feet lies a complex, life-sustaining resource—and some teenagers are already experts at reading it.
why_it_matters: This contest shows that the dirt under your feet isn't just messy—it's a science that determines what food you eat and where you live, and these teenagers are already experts at reading it.

background_read: The National Land and Range Judging Contest has been held in Oklahoma for nearly 75 years, originally starting in the 1950s to teach young farmers practical soil evaluation.

4-H (a youth development program run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, focusing on leadership and life skills) and FFA (Future Farmers of America, a student organization for agricultural education) are key partners in preparing participants for careers in science and agriculture.
Soil judging is a real-world skill used by farmers, engineers, and environmental scientists to decide where to grow crops, build homes, or prevent erosion.
El Reno, Oklahoma, a small city west of Oklahoma City, sits in a region where red clay soil and agriculture are central to the local economy.

perspectives.description: The contest gives students practical skills in earth science and agriculture that classrooms often can't provide. It turns soil into a living laboratory, preparing teenagers for careers in farming, environmental science, and engineering.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / Critical — Limited reach and accessibility
perspectives.description: Events like this mainly serve rural communities and may not be available to urban or low-income students. The focus on traditional agriculture could also overlook other environmental challenges like pollution or climate resilience.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / Analytical — Bridging tradition and modern science
perspectives.description: Soil judging is a centuries-old practice now integrated with modern scientific methods. The contest represents a pattern in agricultural education: combining hands-on tradition with formal analysis to ensure young people remain connected to land-based knowledge.

As the world faces soil degradation and food security challenges, early exposure to soil science could inspire the next generation of conservationists and agronomists. Expanding such programs to more diverse regions could strengthen global sustainability efforts.
